29773-legends-of-the-wailuku:
Charlotte Hapai put these legends into English from tales told by old Hawaiians, with pictures by Will Herwig. The second edition carries a Honolulu copyright of 1920-1921. Hapai dedicates the printed fragment to her grandmother, Harriet Kamakanoenoe Hapai, in memory of happy hours of story-telling. The Wailuku River itself is the thread that binds them.

Fed from the watershed far up Mauna Loa and Mauna Kea, the river roars through the centre of Hilo. Wailuku means destroying water in Hawaiian, and the river earned the name in flood. One legend tells how the dragon Kuna blocked the gorge below Rainbow Falls to drown the goddess Hina in her cave. Her son, the demi-god Maui, came to her rescue.
69328-the-nightless-city-or-the-history-:
J E de Becker wrote The Nightless City, a history of the Yoshiwara district of Tokyo. Becker had lived twenty years in Japan when he wrote. The copy shown is the third edition, revised. Max Nossler and Probsthain sold the book in Yokohama, Shanghai, and London.

The contents map the quarter gate by gate and street by street. Chapters name classes of houses and the tea houses that brought guests in. Dress, hair styles, and room gear of the women get close study. Fees, signs, book keeping, and ads all get pages. So do songs, charms, and the local speech. The book reads as a full record of a licensed quarter and its rules.
britannica-1911-pakokku:
Pakokku, a district in the Minbu division of Upper Burma, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies west of the river Irrawaddy and south of Mandalay. The Chin hills form its west edge as a rule. In 1901 the district held well over three hundred and fifty thousand people.

The land by the two great rivers is rich and flat. Away from them it rises, dry and low, to bare ridges. Millet and sesame are the chief crops, with rice and beans in the wet tracts. Oil fields in the south yield petroleum, and teak comes from held forests. Rain is scant, at times so scant that water is carted for miles. The town of Pakokku, on the Irrawaddy, is the great boat-building hub of Upper Burma.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shi-koku:
Shi-koku, one of Japan's four great islands, covers 7,009 square miles without its smaller dependencies and held 3,199,500 people by the census of 1909. Its name means Four Kingdoms, since from ancient times it was split into Awa in the east, Sanuki in the northeast, Tyo in the northwest, and Tosa in the south. At the Restoration of 1868 the provinces were renamed, and the island now forms the prefectures of Tokushima, Kagawa, Ehime, and Kochi.

Density runs to 176 people per square mile, rising to 418 in Kagawa, higher than in any other prefecture of Japan. The climate is mild and healthy, and Tosa alone in the empire grows two rice crops a year. The land is very mountainous, reaching 6,480 feet at Tshizuchi-Yama in Ehime. People crowd the seacoast. Schools of many kinds abound, but there is no university. Buddhism and Shinto both decline as religious indifference grows among the young.
